claim: E2KO and E3KO mice developed normally and were healthy and fertile.
source: The E2KO and E3KO mice used in this study developed normally and were healthy and fertile.
evidence: This is a direct observation reported in the manuscript about the phenotype of the genetically modified mice.

claim: E2KO and E3KO mice had no differences in body weight at birth and postnatal day 6 compared to control mice.
source: We found no differences in body weight at birth and postnatal (P) day 6, but adult E2KO and E3KO mice were slightly smaller than control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Body weight measurements at specific developmental timepoints are presented in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Adult E2KO and E3KO mice were slightly smaller than control mice.
source: We found no differences in body weight at birth and postnatal (P) day 6, but adult E2KO and E3KO mice were slightly smaller than control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Body mass measurements in adult mice are reported in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Primary murine lung endothelial cells isolated from E3KO mice demonstrated reduced JNK expression compared with MLEC from control mice.
source: Primary murine lung endothelial cells (MLEC) isolated from E3KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E) demonstrated reduced JNK expression compared with MLEC from control mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis showing reduced JNK protein levels in E3KO cells is presented in Figure 1A.

claim: JNK expression by hematopoietic cells was similar in control and E3KO mice.
source: Control studies demonstrated that JNK expression by hematopoietic cells, the number of circulating blood cells, and bone marrow function in transplantation assays were similar in control and E3KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis and flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 demonstrate no differences in JNK expression in hematopoietic cells.

claim: The number of circulating blood cells was similar in control and E3KO mice.
source: Control studies demonstrated that JNK expression by hematopoietic cells, the number of circulating blood cells, and bone marrow function in transplantation assays were similar in control and E3KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Complete blood cell analysis data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C shows no significant differences.

claim: Bone marrow function in transplantation assays was similar in control and E3KO mice.
source: Control studies demonstrated that JNK expression by hematopoietic cells, the number of circulating blood cells, and bone marrow function in transplantation assays were similar in control and E3KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Bone marrow transplantation chimerism data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E shows no significant differences.

claim: JNK was not activated by hypoxia in primary endothelial cells.
source: JNK was not activated by hypoxia or VEGF and both control and E3KO MLEC mounted similar responses to hypoxia and VEGF (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A shows no change in JNK phosphorylation under hypoxic conditions.

claim: JNK was not activated by VEGF in primary endothelial cells.
source: JNK was not activated by hypoxia or VEGF and both control and E3KO MLEC mounted similar responses to hypoxia and VEGF (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B shows no JNK phosphorylation in response to VEGF-A treatment.

claim: Control and E3KO MLEC mounted similar responses to hypoxia.
source: JNK was not activated by hypoxia or VEGF and both control and E3KO MLEC mounted similar responses to hypoxia and VEGF (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Gene expression analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D shows similar upregulation of hypoxia-responsive genes in both genotypes.

claim: Control and E3KO MLEC mounted similar responses to VEGF.
source: JNK was not activated by hypoxia or VEGF and both control and E3KO MLEC mounted similar responses to hypoxia and VEGF (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E shows similar ERK phosphorylation in response to VEGF-A in both genotypes.

claim: Tubulogenesis assays in matrigel demonstrated no differences between control and E3KO MLEC.
source: Tubulogenesis assays in matrigel demonstrated no differences between control and E3KO MLEC and no differences between control and E3KO mice were detected in VEGF-induced microvessel sprouting from collagen-embedded aortic rings (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: Images and quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A show similar tubular network formation.

claim: No differences between control and E3KO mice were detected in VEGF-induced microvessel sprouting from collagen-embedded aortic rings.
source: Tubulogenesis assays in matrigel demonstrated no differences between control and E3KO MLEC and no differences between control and E3KO mice were detected in VEGF-induced microvessel sprouting from collagen-embedded aortic rings (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: Confocal images and quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B show similar microvessel numbers.

claim: No differences in proliferation were found between control and E3KO MLEC.
source: We also found no differences in proliferation or migration between control and E3KO MLEC (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C–E).
evidence: EdU incorporation and Ki-67 staining data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C,D show no significant differences.

claim: No differences in migration were found between control and E3KO MLEC.
source: We also found no differences in proliferation or migration between control and E3KO MLEC (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C–E).
evidence: Scratch assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4E shows similar wound closure rates.

claim: No differences in choroidal neovascularization between control and E3KO mice were observed following laser-induced injury of the eye.
source: To assess angiogenesis in vivo, we examined laser-induced injury of the eye; no differences in choroidal neovascularization between control and E3KO mice were observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: Confocal images and quantification of CNV area in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B show no significant differences.

claim: No differences in tumor angiogenesis between control and E3KO mice were found.
source: Similarly, we found no differences in tumor angiogenesis between control and E3KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C–F).
evidence: Tumor mass measurements and vessel quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 5C-F show no significant differences.

claim: JNK in endothelial cells is not required for angiogenesis in vitro or in vivo in adult mice.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that JNK in endothelial cells is not required for angiogenesis in vitro or in vivo in adult mice.
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple in vitro and in vivo angiogenesis assays showing no differences between control and JNK-deficient mice.

claim: Laser Doppler imaging revealed approximately 80% decreased blood perfusion to the ligated limbs of control mice following femoral artery ligation.
source: Laser Doppler imaging revealed ~80% decreased blood perfusion to the ligated limbs of control mice; blood perfusion was restored to ~60% of the contralateral limbs by day 3 (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Quantitative laser Doppler data in Figure 1C,D shows the extent of blood flow reduction.

claim: Blood perfusion was restored to approximately 60% of the contralateral limbs by day 3 post-FAL in control mice.
source: Laser Doppler imaging revealed ~80% decreased blood perfusion to the ligated limbs of control mice; blood perfusion was restored to ~60% of the contralateral limbs by day 3 (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Quantitative laser Doppler data in Figure 1C,D shows blood flow recovery over time.

claim: Control mice did not exhibit major hallmarks of ischemia following femoral artery ligation.
source: These mice did not exhibit major hallmarks of ischemia (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: Ischemia and movement scores in Figure 1E-G show minimal tissue damage in control mice.

claim: E3KO mice showed complete blockade of blood flow following femoral artery occlusion.
source: In contrast, E3KO mice showed complete blockade of blood flow following occlusion (Figure 1C,D) leading to severe necrosis (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: Laser Doppler imaging data in Figure 1C,D shows near-complete loss of blood perfusion in E3KO mice.

claim: E3KO mice developed severe necrosis following femoral artery occlusion.
source: In contrast, E3KO mice showed complete blockade of blood flow following occlusion (Figure 1C,D) leading to severe necrosis (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: Images and ischemia scores in Figure 1E-G show severe tissue damage in E3KO mice.

claim: Ligation of the femoral artery more proximally at its origin demonstrated increased blood flow blockade and failure to recover in both E2KO and E3KO mice.
source: Ligation of the FA more proximally at its origin (a more severe form of FAL) also demonstrated increased blood flow blockade and failure to recover in both E2KO and E3KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A–C).
evidence: Laser Doppler data in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A-C shows impaired blood flow recovery in JNK-deficient mice.

claim: No post-FAL phenotype was detected in mice with JNK1 or JNK2-deficiency alone.
source: In contrast, no post-FAL phenotype was detected in mice with JNK1 or JNK2-deficiency alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 6D) or in mice with JNK1 plus JNK2-deficiency in hematopoietic cells or muscle (Figure 1—figure supplement 6G–I).
evidence: Laser Doppler data in Figure 1—figure supplement 6D shows normal blood flow recovery in single JNK knockout mice.

claim: No post-FAL phenotype was detected in mice with JNK1 plus JNK2-deficiency in hematopoietic cells or muscle.
source: In contrast, no post-FAL phenotype was detected in mice with JNK1 or JNK2-deficiency alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 6D) or in mice with JNK1 plus JNK2-deficiency in hematopoietic cells or muscle (Figure 1—figure supplement 6G–I).
evidence: Laser Doppler data in Figure 1—figure supplement 6G-I shows normal blood flow recovery in tissue-specific JNK knockout mice.

claim: JNK1/2 in endothelial cells play a key role in the response to arterial occlusion.
source: These data suggest that JNK1/2 in endothelial cells play a key role in the response to arterial occlusion.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that endothelial-specific JNK deficiency causes severe post-FAL phenotype, while deficiency in other cell types does not.

claim: Coronary artery occlusion caused significantly greater mortality of E3KO mice compared with control mice.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, coronary artery occlusion caused significantly greater mortality of E3KO mice compared with control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 6E,F).
evidence: Survival curve data in Figure 1—figure supplement 6F shows decreased survival in E3KO mice after coronary artery ligation.

claim: No changes in blood pressure were detected in E3KO mice compared to control mice.
source: The defect in blood flow of E3KO mice post-FAL could be mediated by cardiovascular dysfunction, but no changes in blood pressure, heart rate, or echocardiographic measurements of cardiac function were detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 7A–C).
evidence: Blood pressure measurements in Figure 1—figure supplement 7A,B show no significant differences.

claim: No changes in heart rate were detected in E3KO mice compared to control mice.
source: The defect in blood flow of E3KO mice post-FAL could be mediated by cardiovascular dysfunction, but no changes in blood pressure, heart rate, or echocardiographic measurements of cardiac function were detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 7A–C).
evidence: Heart rate measurements in Figure 1—figure supplement 7A,B show no significant differences.

claim: No changes in echocardiographic measurements of cardiac function were detected in E3KO mice compared to control mice.
source: The defect in blood flow of E3KO mice post-FAL could be mediated by cardiovascular dysfunction, but no changes in blood pressure, heart rate, or echocardiographic measurements of cardiac function were detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 7A–C).
evidence: Echocardiographic data in Figure 1—figure supplement 7C shows no significant differences in cardiac function parameters.

claim: Contraction and endothelium-dependent relaxation responses in aortic explants from E3KO and control mice were similar.
source: Moreover, contraction and endothelium-dependent relaxation responses in aortic explants from E3KO and control mice were similar (Figure 1—figure supplement 7D).
evidence: Myograph data in Figure 1—figure supplement 7D shows similar vasocontraction and vasorelaxation responses.

claim: Neither cardiovascular dysfunction nor defective vasodilatory responses contribute to the post-FAL phenotype of E3KO mice.
source: These data indicate that neither cardiovascular dysfunction nor defective vasodilatory responses contribute to the post-FAL phenotype of E3KO mice.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the absence of cardiovascular and vascular function defects in E3KO mice.

claim: The early and severe blood perfusion blockade in E3KO mice post-FAL suggests a defect in collateral artery function.
source: The early and severe blood perfusion blockade in E3KO mice post-FAL suggests a defect in collateral artery function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing and severity of blood flow blockade observed in E3KO mice.

claim: Gracilis collaterals were identified as two lumenized continuous arteries that connected the PCFA to the saphenous artery in control mice.
source: Gracilis collaterals were identified as two lumenized continuous arteries that connected the PCFA to the saphenous artery (SA) (Figure 1H) and expanded radially during the post-FAL response (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: Microfil perfusion images in Figure 1H show the anatomical structure of gracilis collaterals.

claim: Gracilis collaterals expanded radially during the post-FAL response in control mice.
source: Gracilis collaterals were identified as two lumenized continuous arteries that connected the PCFA to the saphenous artery (SA) (Figure 1H) and expanded radially during the post-FAL response (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and quantification in Figure 1H,I shows increased collateral artery diameter post-FAL.

claim: Gracilis collateral arteries were abnormal in E3KO mice.
source: In contrast, these arteries were abnormal in E3KO mice; arteries emerged from the PCFA and SA (Figure 1H), but were thin and branched into multiple smaller vessels forming a disorganized network (Figure 1H).
evidence: Microfil perfusion images in Figure 1H show abnormal vascular patterning in E3KO mice.

claim: Arteries emerged from the PCFA and SA in E3KO mice but were thin and branched into multiple smaller vessels forming a disorganized network.
source: In contrast, these arteries were abnormal in E3KO mice; arteries emerged from the PCFA and SA (Figure 1H), but were thin and branched into multiple smaller vessels forming a disorganized network (Figure 1H).
evidence: Microfil perfusion images in Figure 1H show the morphological abnormalities of vessels in E3KO mice.

claim: Micro-computed tomography analysis confirmed reduced collateral artery size and continuity in the limbs of E3KO mice.
source: Micro-computed tomography (μCT) analysis confirmed reduced collateral artery size and continuity in the limbs of E3KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 8A).
evidence: μCT images in Figure 1—figure supplement 8A show reduced vascular continuity in E3KO mice.

claim: Collateral artery defects may contribute to decreased blood flow and increased hypoxia in post-FAL E3KO mice, despite no overall reduction in muscle vascularization or macrophage recruitment.
source: These collateral artery defects may contribute to decreased blood flow and increased hypoxia in post-FAL E3KO mice, despite no overall reduction in muscle vascularization or macrophage recruitment (Figure 1—figure supplement 8B–E).
evidence: Gene expression data in Figure 1—figure supplement 8B-E shows similar endothelial cell markers and macrophage markers in both genotypes.

claim: Map3k10 and Map3k11 were the most highly expressed members of the MLK group in endothelial cells.
source: Gene expression analysis demonstrated that Map3k10 and Map3k11 were the most highly expressed members of this group in endothelial cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: RNA-seq data in Figure 2A shows FPKM values for different MLK family members.

claim: Map3k10-/- Map3k11-/- MLEC exhibited reduced phosphorylation of the JNK substrate cJun compared with control MLEC.
source: Indeed, Map3k10-/- Map3k11-/- MLEC exhibited reduced phosphorylation of the JNK substrate cJun compared with control MLEC (Figure 2B).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis in Figure 2B shows decreased p-cJun levels in MLK-deficient cells.

claim: MLK-deficient mice showed increased blood flow blockade following femoral artery ligation.
source: Similar to E3KO mice, MLK-deficient mice showed increased blood flow blockade, failure of blood flow restoration by day 3 post-FAL, and necrosis (Figure 2C–G).
evidence: Laser Doppler data in Figure 2C,D shows severe blood perfusion blockade in MLK-deficient mice.

claim: MLK-deficient mice showed failure of blood flow restoration by day 3 post-FAL.
source: Similar to E3KO mice, MLK-deficient mice showed increased blood flow blockade, failure of blood flow restoration by day 3 post-FAL, and necrosis (Figure 2C–G).
evidence: Laser Doppler data in Figure 2C,D shows no blood flow recovery in MLK-deficient mice.

claim: MLK-deficient mice developed necrosis following femoral artery ligation.
source: Similar to E3KO mice, MLK-deficient mice showed increased blood flow blockade, failure of blood flow restoration by day 3 post-FAL, and necrosis (Figure 2C–G).
evidence: Images and ischemia scores in Figure 2E-G show severe tissue damage in MLK-deficient mice.

claim: Abnormal gracilis collateral arteries were found in Map3k10-/- Map3k11-/- mice.
source: Moreover, we found abnormal gracilis collateral arteries in Map3k10-/- Map3k11-/- mice (Figures 2H and 3A).
evidence: Microfil perfusion images in Figure 2H and confocal images in Figure 3A show abnormal collateral artery patterning.

claim: The MLK-JNK signaling pathway in endothelial cells is important for collateral artery patterning and the post-FAL response.
source: These data demonstrate that the MLK-JNK signaling pathway in endothelial cells is important for collateral artery patterning and the post-FAL response.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the similar phenotypes observed in both JNK-deficient and MLK-deficient mice.

claim: The abdominal muscle vasculature of Map3k10-/-Map3k11-/- mice shows very few arteriole-to-arteriole interconnections.
source: The abdominal muscle vasculature of Map3k10-/-Map3k11-/- mice shows very few arteriole-to-arteriole interconnections. Quantitation reveals significantly reduced arteriolar arcade numbers in Map3k10-/-Map3k11-/- mice compared to WT mice (mean ± SEM; n = 5 mice).
evidence: Stereomicroscope images and quantification in Figure 3B show reduced arteriolar arcades in MLK-deficient mice.

claim: Compound Mapk8/9/10 gene ablation in adult mice did not alter the post-FAL response.
source: We found that compound Mapk8/9/10 gene ablation in adult mice did not alter the post-FAL response (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Laser Doppler data in Figure 4A-D shows normal blood flow recovery in tamoxifen-treated adult mice.

claim: Compound Mapk8/9/10 gene ablation in embryos prior to FAL in adult mice caused increased blood flow blockade post FAL and failure to recover.
source: In contrast, compound Mapk8/9/10 gene ablation in embryos prior to FAL in adult mice caused increased blood flow blockade post FAL and failure to recover (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: Laser Doppler data in Figure 4E-G shows impaired blood flow recovery in mice with embryonic JNK deletion.

claim: The post-FAL phenotype of E3KO mice is caused by an early developmental defect.
source: These data demonstrate that the post-FAL phenotype of E3KO mice is caused by an early developmental defect.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the differential effects of adult versus embryonic JNK deletion on post-FAL response.

claim: The gracilis collaterals in post-natal day 6 (P6) and P0 control mice interconnected the PCFA and the SA.
source: We found that the gracilis collaterals in post-natal day 6 (P6) and P0 control mice interconnected the PCFA and the SA (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Confocal images in Figure 5A,B show continuous collateral arteries connecting PCFA to SA.

claim: Dil perfusion analysis demonstrated that the gracilis collateral arteries had lumens.
source: Dil perfusion analysis demonstrated that the arteries had lumens (Figure 5A,B) and were fully covered by smooth muscle cells at P6 (Figure 5A; SMA), but not at P0 (Figure 5B; SMA).
evidence: Dil perfusion images in Figure 5A,B show lumenized vessels.

claim: Gracilis collateral arteries were fully covered by smooth muscle cells at P6.
source: Dil perfusion analysis demonstrated that the arteries had lumens (Figure 5A,B) and were fully covered by smooth muscle cells at P6 (Figure 5A; SMA), but not at P0 (Figure 5B; SMA).
evidence: SMA staining in Figure 5A shows smooth muscle coverage at P6.

claim: Gracilis collateral arteries were not fully covered by smooth muscle cells at P0.
source: Dil perfusion analysis demonstrated that the arteries had lumens (Figure 5A,B) and were fully covered by smooth muscle cells at P6 (Figure 5A; SMA), but not at P0 (Figure 5B; SMA).
evidence: SMA staining in Figure 5B shows lack of smooth muscle coverage at P0.

claim: Gracilis collaterals in E3KO mice were not formed at P6 or P0.
source: In contrast, gracilis collaterals in E3KO mice were not formed at P6 or P0 (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Confocal images in Figure 5A,B show absence of continuous collateral arteries in E3KO mice.

claim: Individual vessels emerged from the PCFA and the SA in E3KO mice but instead of interconnecting to form collaterals, these vessels branched off into multiple smaller caliber vessels.
source: Individual vessels did emerge from the PCFA and the SA, but instead of interconnecting to form collaterals, these vessels branched off into multiple smaller caliber vessels (Figure 5A,B; Dil Perfusion) that lacked smooth muscle coverage at P6 (Figure 5A; SMA) and appeared to continue into the capillary circulation (Figure 5A,B; Dil Perfusion).
evidence: Dil perfusion images in Figure 5A,B show branching vessels in E3KO mice.

claim: Vessels emerging from the PCFA and SA in E3KO mice lacked smooth muscle coverage at P6.
source: Individual vessels did emerge from the PCFA and the SA, but instead of interconnecting to form collaterals, these vessels branched off into multiple smaller caliber vessels (Figure 5A,B; Dil Perfusion) that lacked smooth muscle coverage at P6 (Figure 5A; SMA) and appeared to continue into the capillary circulation (Figure 5A,B; Dil Perfusion).
evidence: SMA staining in Figure 5A shows lack of smooth muscle coverage on vessels in E3KO mice.

claim: Vessels emerging from the PCFA and SA in E3KO mice appeared to continue into the capillary circulation.
source: Individual vessels did emerge from the PCFA and the SA, but instead of interconnecting to form collaterals, these vessels branched off into multiple smaller caliber vessels (Figure 5A,B; Dil Perfusion) that lacked smooth muscle coverage at P6 (Figure 5A; SMA) and appeared to continue into the capillary circulation (Figure 5A,B; Dil Perfusion).
evidence: Dil perfusion images in Figure 5A,B show vessels connecting to capillary networks.

claim: Analysis of the abdominal muscle arterial circulation in P0 pups revealed numerous arteriolar arcades in control mice.
source: Similarly, analysis of the abdominal muscle arterial circulation in P0 pups revealed numerous arteriolar arcades (direct arteriole-to-arteriole interconnections) in control mice, but this arterial patterning was significantly reduced in E3KO mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: Stereomicroscope images and quantification in Figure 5C show arteriolar arcades in control mice.

claim: Arterial patterning in the abdominal muscle was significantly reduced in E3KO mice compared to control mice at P0.
source: Similarly, analysis of the abdominal muscle arterial circulation in P0 pups revealed numerous arteriolar arcades (direct arteriole-to-arteriole interconnections) in control mice, but this arterial patterning was significantly reduced in E3KO mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: Stereomicroscope images and quantification in Figure 5C show reduced arteriolar arcades in E3KO mice.

claim: Defects in gracilis collateral and abdominal arteriolar arcade development were detected in MLK-deficient mice.
source: These defects in gracilis collateral and abdominal arteriolar arcade development were also detected in MLK-deficient mice (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Confocal and stereomicroscope images in Figure 3A,B show similar vascular defects in MLK-deficient mice.

claim: Large caliber vessels, including the FA/SA and PCFA, were established at E16.5.
source: While large caliber vessels, including the FA/SA and PCFA, were established (Figure 5D,E), distinct collaterals directly interconnecting the PCFA and SA were not formed at E16.5 and the gracilis muscle was covered by a capillary plexus (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: Confocal images in Figure 5D,E show major arteries at E16.5.

claim: Distinct collaterals directly interconnecting the PCFA and SA were not formed at E16.5.
source: While large caliber vessels, including the FA/SA and PCFA, were established (Figure 5D,E), distinct collaterals directly interconnecting the PCFA and SA were not formed at E16.5 and the gracilis muscle was covered by a capillary plexus (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: Confocal images in Figure 5D,E show absence of distinct collaterals at E16.5.

claim: The gracilis muscle was covered by a capillary plexus at E16.5.
source: While large caliber vessels, including the FA/SA and PCFA, were established (Figure 5D,E), distinct collaterals directly interconnecting the PCFA and SA were not formed at E16.5 and the gracilis muscle was covered by a capillary plexus (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: Confocal images in Figure 5D,E show capillary plexus covering the gracilis muscle.

claim: Prominent vessels emerge from the PCFA and the SA at E16.5.
source: Prominent vessels do emerge from the PCFA and the SA (Figure 5E), but did not extend along the gracilis muscle as distinct collaterals; instead, these vessels branched and appeared to continue into the capillary plexus (Figure 5E).
evidence: Confocal images in Figure 5E show vessels emerging from major arteries.

claim: Vessels emerging from the PCFA and SA at E16.5 did not extend along the gracilis muscle as distinct collaterals but branched and appeared to continue into the capillary plexus.
source: Prominent vessels do emerge from the PCFA and the SA (Figure 5E), but did not extend along the gracilis muscle as distinct collaterals; instead, these vessels branched and appeared to continue into the capillary plexus (Figure 5E).
evidence: Confocal images in Figure 5E show vessels connecting to the capillary plexus.

claim: Gracilis collaterals may form through a plexus intermediate.
source: Gracilis collaterals may therefore form through a plexus intermediate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that a capillary plexus exists at E16.5 before distinct collaterals are formed.

claim: Remodeling of vessels within the capillary plexus likely leads to the formation of collateral arteries in close apposition to nerve fibres.
source: Remodeling of vessels within this plexus likely leads to the formation of collateral arteries in close apposition to nerve fibres (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Confocal images in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 show collateral arteries associated with nerves.

claim: The process of collateral artery maturation appears to start at the two distal ends, where the future gracilis collaterals emerge from the PCFA and the SA and continue toward the middle of the muscle.
source: This process of maturation appears to start at the two distal ends, where the future gracilis collaterals emerge from the PCFA and the SA (Figure 5E, arrowheads) and continue toward the middle of the muscle; a pattern of remodeling that likely reflects the blood flow characteristics of these vessels (Meisner et al., 2013).
evidence: Confocal images in Figure 5E show prominent vessels at the ends of the gracilis muscle.

claim: The pattern of collateral artery remodeling likely reflects the blood flow characteristics of these vessels.
source: This process of maturation appears to start at the two distal ends, where the future gracilis collaterals emerge from the PCFA and the SA (Figure 5E, arrowheads) and continue toward the middle of the muscle; a pattern of remodeling that likely reflects the blood flow characteristics of these vessels (Meisner et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to previous work on vascular remodeling.

claim: The gracilis muscle capillary plexus in E16.5 E3KO embryos was hyperbranched, denser, and disorganized with vessels of variable width that elaborated more filopodia than control embryos.
source: Studies of E16.5 E3KO embryos demonstrated that the gracilis muscle capillary plexus was hyperbranched, denser, and disorganized with vessels of variable width that elaborated more filopodia than control embryos (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: Confocal images in Figure 5D,E show abnormal capillary plexus morphology in E3KO embryos.

claim: The failure of collateral artery formation in E3KO mice may be caused by defective sprouting angiogenesis that initially generates a hyperbranched, denser, and more chaotically organized plexus that fails to properly remodel.
source: This observation suggests that the failure of collateral artery formation in E3KO mice may be caused by defective sprouting angiogenesis that initially generates a hyperbranched, denser, and more chaotically organized plexus that fails to properly remodel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed abnormalities in the capillary plexus of E3KO embryos.

claim: Analysis of retinal flatmounts from P6 E3KO mice demonstrated significantly reduced radial extension of the vascular plexus.
source: Analysis of retinal flatmounts from P6 E3KO mice demonstrated significantly reduced radial extension of the vascular plexus (Figure 6A–C,L).
evidence: Confocal images and quantification in Figure 6A-C,L show reduced vascularized retinal area in E3KO mice.

claim: The growing angiogenic front of E3KO retinas showed higher vascular density compared to littermate control mice.
source: Closer examination demonstrated higher vascular density in the growing angiogenic front of the mutant retinas compared to littermate control mice (Figure 6D–G,H,J,M).
evidence: Confocal images and quantification in Figure 6D-G,H,J,M show increased vascular density in E3KO retinas.

claim: No differences in vessel pericyte coverage were found between control and E3KO retinas.
source: We found no differences in vessel pericyte coverage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1); however, the angiogenic front of the mutant retinas included larger numbers of tip cells and a larger number of filopodia (Figure 6H–K,N,O).
evidence: Confocal images in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 show similar pericyte coverage in both genotypes.

claim: The angiogenic front of E3KO retinas included larger numbers of tip cells.
source: We found no differences in vessel pericyte coverage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1); however, the angiogenic front of the mutant retinas included larger numbers of tip cells and a larger number of filopodia (Figure 6H–K,N,O).
evidence: Confocal images and quantification in Figure 6H-K,N show increased tip cell numbers in E3KO retinas.

claim: The angiogenic front of E3KO retinas included a larger number of filopodia.
source: We found no differences in vessel pericyte coverage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1); however, the angiogenic front of the mutant retinas included larger numbers of tip cells and a larger number of filopodia (Figure 6H–K,N,O).
evidence: Confocal images and quantification in Figure 6H-K,O show increased filopodia numbers in E3KO retinas.

claim: Similar retinal vascular defects were obtained from analysis of E2KO and Map3k10-/- Map3k11-/- mice.
source: Similar data were obtained from analysis of E2KO and Map3k10-/- Map3k11-/- mice (Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: Confocal images and quantification in Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3 show similar phenotypes in E2KO and MLK-deficient mice.

claim: The MLK-JNK signaling pathway restrains excessive endothelial cell sprouting during developmental angiogenesis.
source: These data confirm that the MLK-JNK signaling pathway restrains excessive endothelial cell sprouting during developmental angiogenesis.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the hypersprouting phenotype observed in JNK-deficient and MLK-deficient retinas.

claim: 781 genes were differentially expressed between E3KO and control endothelial cells.
source: We found 781 genes that were differentially expressed between E3KO and control endothelial cells.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis comparing gene expression between genotypes.

claim: Gene ontology analysis demonstrated significant enrichment for several biological processes, including vascular development and morphogenesis.
source: Gene ontology analysis demonstrated significant enrichment for several biological processes, including vascular development and morphogenesis, and we identified 64 differentially expressed genes that might contribute to vascular defects (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis results are presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 64 differentially expressed genes were identified that might contribute to vascular defects.
source: Gene ontology analysis demonstrated significant enrichment for several biological processes, including vascular development and morphogenesis, and we identified 64 differentially expressed genes that might contribute to vascular defects (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: A heatmap of vascular-related differentially expressed genes is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Differentially expressed genes included components of the Notch signaling pathway, including Dll4, Hey1, Hes1, and Lfng.
source: These genes included components of the Notch signaling pathway; for example, Dll4, Hey1, Hes1, and Lfng (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: qRT-PCR data in Figure 7A and immunofluorescence in Figure 7B show reduced expression of Notch pathway genes.

claim: The Notch pathway plays a major role during developmental angiogenesis, including tip/stalk cell specification and endothelial cell sprouting.
source: This may be significant because the Notch pathway plays a major role during developmental angiogenesis, including tip/stalk cell specification and endothelial cell sprouting (Roca and Adams, 2007; Phng and Gerhardt, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The hypersprouting defects observed in E2KO, E3KO and Map3k10-/- Map3k11-/- mice resemble those previously reported for mice with reduced Dll4/Notch signaling.
source: Indeed, the hypersprouting defects observed in E2KO, E3KO and Map3k10-/- Map3k11-/- mice resemble those previously reported for mice with reduced Dll4/Notch signaling (Hellström et al., 2007; Suchting et al., 2007; Benedito et al., 2009), including Lfng-/- mice (Benedito et al., 2009).
evidence: This comparison is based on similarities to published phenotypes of Notch pathway mutants.

claim: Dll4-/+ mice display perturbations in collateral artery formation.
source: Moreover, Dll4-/+ mice display perturbations in collateral artery formation and, like Notch1-/+ mice (Takeshita et al., 2007), show reduced recovery of blood perfusion in models of vascular occlusion (Cristofaro et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on published studies of Dll4 heterozygous mice.

claim: Dll4-/+ mice show reduced recovery of blood perfusion in models of vascular occlusion.
source: Moreover, Dll4-/+ mice display perturbations in collateral artery formation and, like Notch1-/+ mice (Takeshita et al., 2007), show reduced recovery of blood perfusion in models of vascular occlusion (Cristofaro et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on published studies of Dll4 heterozygous mice.

claim: Notch1-/+ mice show reduced recovery of blood perfusion in models of vascular occlusion.
source: Moreover, Dll4-/+ mice display perturbations in collateral artery formation and, like Notch1-/+ mice (Takeshita et al., 2007), show reduced recovery of blood perfusion in models of vascular occlusion (Cristofaro et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on published studies of Notch1 heterozygous mice.

claim: Treatment of endothelial cells with VEGF caused increased expression of Dll4 protein.
source: Treatment of endothelial cells with VEGF or bFGF caused increased expression of Dll4 protein and promoted accumulation of the Notch intracellular domain (NICD). However, these responses were suppressed in JNK-deficient endothelial cells (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis in Figure 7C shows increased Dll4 protein in VEGF-treated control cells.

claim: Treatment of endothelial cells with bFGF caused increased expression of Dll4 protein.
source: Treatment of endothelial cells with VEGF or bFGF caused increased expression of Dll4 protein and promoted accumulation of the Notch intracellular domain (NICD). However, these responses were suppressed in JNK-deficient endothelial cells (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis in Figure 7D shows increased Dll4 protein in bFGF-treated control cells.

claim: Treatment of endothelial cells with VEGF promoted accumulation of the Notch intracellular domain (NICD).
source: Treatment of endothelial cells with VEGF or bFGF caused increased expression of Dll4 protein and promoted accumulation of the Notch intracellular domain (NICD). However, these responses were suppressed in JNK-deficient endothelial cells (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis in Figure 7C shows increased NICD in VEGF-treated control cells.

claim: Treatment of endothelial cells with bFGF promoted accumulation of the Notch intracellular domain (NICD).
source: Treatment of endothelial cells with VEGF or bFGF caused increased expression of Dll4 protein and promoted accumulation of the Notch intracellular domain (NICD). However, these responses were suppressed in JNK-deficient endothelial cells (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis in Figure 7D shows increased NICD in bFGF-treated control cells.

claim: VEGF-induced Dll4 expression and NICD accumulation were suppressed in JNK-deficient endothelial cells.
source: Treatment of endothelial cells with VEGF or bFGF caused increased expression of Dll4 protein and promoted accumulation of the Notch intracellular domain (NICD). However, these responses were suppressed in JNK-deficient endothelial cells (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis in Figure 7C shows reduced Dll4 and NICD in VEGF-treated JNK-deficient cells.

claim: bFGF-induced Dll4 expression and NICD accumulation were suppressed in JNK-deficient endothelial cells.
source: Treatment of endothelial cells with VEGF or bFGF caused increased expression of Dll4 protein and promoted accumulation of the Notch intracellular domain (NICD). However, these responses were suppressed in JNK-deficient endothelial cells (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis in Figure 7D shows reduced Dll4 and NICD in bFGF-treated JNK-deficient cells.

claim: Reduced Dll4 protein expression by E3KO endothelial cells was observed in vitro and in vivo.
source: Indeed, reduced Dll4 protein expression by E3KO endothelial cells was observed in vitro and in vivo (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data in Figure 7B,E shows reduced Dll4 expression in cultured cells and retinal tissue.

claim: JNK can promote Notch signaling in endothelial cells by regulating Dll4 expression.
source: These data indicate that JNK can promote Notch signaling in endothelial cells by regulating Dll4 expression.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observed reduction in Dll4 expression and NICD accumulation in JNK-deficient cells.

claim: JNK is not required for angiogenesis in vitro or in adult mice.
source: We did not find that JNK signaling was required for angiogenesis in vitro or in adult mice, but JNK signaling is required for proper vascular morphogenesis and the normal formation of collateral arteries in muscle.
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple angiogenesis assays showing no defects in JNK-deficient mice.

claim: JNK signaling is required for proper vascular morphogenesis.
source: We did not find that JNK signaling was required for angiogenesis in vitro or in adult mice, but JNK signaling is required for proper vascular morphogenesis and the normal formation of collateral arteries in muscle.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observed vascular patterning defects in JNK-deficient mice during development.

claim: JNK signaling is required for the normal formation of collateral arteries in muscle.
source: We did not find that JNK signaling was required for angiogenesis in vitro or in adult mice, but JNK signaling is required for proper vascular morphogenesis and the normal formation of collateral arteries in muscle.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the absence of functional collateral arteries in JNK-deficient mice.

claim: Disruption of the mixed-lineage protein kinase (MLK) - cJun NH2-terminal kinase (JNK) signaling pathway in endothelial cells causes severe blockade of blood flow and failure to recover in the murine femoral artery ligation model of hindlimb ischemia.
source: We report that disruption of the mixed-lineage protein kinase (MLK) - cJun NH2-terminal kinase (JNK) signaling pathway in endothelial cells causes severe blockade of blood flow and failure to recover in the murine femoral artery ligation model of hindlimb ischemia.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding reported in the abstract.

claim: The MLK-JNK pathway is required for the formation of native collateral arteries that can restore circulation following arterial occlusion.
source: We show that the MLK-JNK pathway is required for the formation of native collateral arteries that can restore circulation following arterial occlusion.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Disruption of the MLK-JNK pathway causes decreased Dll4/Notch signaling.
source: Disruption of the MLK-JNK pathway causes decreased Dll4/Notch signaling, excessive sprouting angiogenesis, and defects in developmental vascular morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the mechanistic findings reported in the abstract.

claim: Disruption of the MLK-JNK pathway causes excessive sprouting angiogenesis.
source: Disruption of the MLK-JNK pathway causes decreased Dll4/Notch signaling, excessive sprouting angiogenesis, and defects in developmental vascular morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the mechanistic findings reported in the abstract.

claim: Disruption of the MLK-JNK pathway causes defects in developmental vascular morphogenesis.
source: Disruption of the MLK-JNK pathway causes decreased Dll4/Notch signaling, excessive sprouting angiogenesis, and defects in developmental vascular morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the mechanistic findings reported in the abstract.

claim: The MLK-JNK signaling pathway is a key regulatory mechanism that protects against ischemia in arterial occlusive disease.
source: Our analysis demonstrates that the MLK-JNK signaling pathway is a key regulatory mechanism that protects against ischemia in arterial occlusive disease.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: Collaterals are artery-to-artery or arteriole-to-arteriole interconnections that can bypass an occlusion by providing an alternative route for blood flow to the affected tissue.
source: Collaterals are artery-to-artery or arteriole-to-arteriole interconnections that can bypass an occlusion by providing an alternative route for blood flow to the affected tissue that restores tissue homeostasis and limits tissue damage (Antoniucci et al., 2002; Schaper, 2009; Faber et al., 2014; Simons and Eichmann, 2015).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Clinical outcome in patients with arterial occlusion depends on the presence of an adequate collateral circulation.
source: Indeed, clinical outcome in patients with arterial occlusion depends on the presence of an adequate collateral circulation and animal models of arterial occlusion provide strong evidence for the critical importance of the extent of the native (pre-existing) collateral circulation in restoring blood perfusion and limiting ischemic sequelae following arterial occlusion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the clinical importance of collateral circulation.

claim: Animal models of arterial occlusion provide strong evidence for the critical importance of the extent of the native collateral circulation in restoring blood perfusion and limiting ischemic sequelae following arterial occlusion.
source: Indeed, clinical outcome in patients with arterial occlusion depends on the presence of an adequate collateral circulation and animal models of arterial occlusion provide strong evidence for the critical importance of the extent of the native (pre-existing) collateral circulation in restoring blood perfusion and limiting ischemic sequelae following arterial occlusion.
evidence: This is established knowledge from animal model studies.

claim: Following arterial occlusion, more blood flow is diverted to the collateral circulation and this increased flow and sheer stress in collateral arteries initiates a number of processes that result in the outward remodeling (arteriogenesis) of these vessels into efficient conductance arteries.
source: Following arterial occlusion, more blood flow is diverted to the collateral circulation and this increased flow and sheer stress in collateral arteries initiates a number of processes that result in the outward remodeling (arteriogenesis) of these vessels into efficient conductance arteries (Heil et al., 2006; Schaper, 2009; van Royen et al., 2009; Simons and Eichmann, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about arteriogenesis supported by citations.

claim: Collateral artery remodeling involves multiple cellular processes, including endothelial cell activation and proliferation, monocyte/macrophage recruitment and smooth muscle cell proliferation.
source: Collateral artery remodeling involves multiple cellular processes, including endothelial cell activation and proliferation, monocyte/macrophage recruitment and smooth muscle cell proliferation, all of which contribute to increased collateral artery diameter, including increased thickness of the tunica media.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the cellular processes involved in arteriogenesis.

claim: Little is known about the cellular and morphogenetic processes, or the molecular factors and mechanisms, that contribute to native collateral artery formation.
source: Although the collateral circulation is crucially important for the protective response to arterial occlusive diseases, little is known about the cellular and morphogenetic processes, or the molecular factors and mechanisms, that contribute to native collateral artery formation (Antoniucci et al., 2002; Schaper, 2009; Faber et al., 2014; Simons and Eichmann, 2015).
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Murine pial collaterals are established during embryonic development with some remodeling and maturation continuing postnatally.
source: However, studies of leptomenengial (or pial) collateral arteries in the brain have provided significant insight. Murine pial collaterals are established during embryonic development with some remodeling and maturation continuing postnatally.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pial collateral development.

claim: The process of native collateral artery formation during embryogenesis has been termed collaterogenesis.
source: The process of native collateral artery formation during embryogenesis has been termed collaterogenesis and involves a number of molecules including, platelet-endothelial cell adhesion molecule 1 (PECAM1) (Chen et al., 2010), gap junction protein, connexin37 (Cx37) (Fang et al., 2011, 2012), prolyl hydroxylase domain-containing protein 2 (PHD2) (Takeda et al., 2011), endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) (Dai and Faber, 2010), chloride intracellular channel 4 (CLIC4) (Chalothorn et al., 2009), and Synectin (Moraes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a definition and summary of known molecules involved in collaterogenesis, supported by citations.

claim: Collaterogenesis involves a number of molecules including PECAM1, Cx37, PHD2, eNOS, CLIC4, and Synectin.
source: The process of native collateral artery formation during embryogenesis has been termed collaterogenesis and involves a number of molecules including, platelet-endothelial cell adhesion molecule 1 (PECAM1) (Chen et al., 2010), gap junction protein, connexin37 (Cx37) (Fang et al., 2011, 2012), prolyl hydroxylase domain-containing protein 2 (PHD2) (Takeda et al., 2011), endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) (Dai and Faber, 2010), chloride intracellular channel 4 (CLIC4) (Chalothorn et al., 2009), and Synectin (Moraes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Signaling pathways that have been reported to contribute to collaterogenesis include NF-κB, VEGF, and the Dll4 – Notch pathway.
source: Signaling pathways that have been reported to contribute to collaterogenesis include NF-κB (Tirziu et al., 2012), VEGF (Chalothorn et al., 2007; Lucitti et al., 2012), and the Dll4 – Notch pathway (Cristofaro et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: JNK is a signaling pathway that has been reported to play major roles in angiogenic responses.
source: The purpose of this study was to examine the role of the c-Jun NH2-terminal kinase (JNK) (Davis, 2000), a signaling pathway that has been reported to play major roles in angiogenic responses (Jiménez et al., 2001; Ennis et al., 2005; Medhora et al., 2008; Uchida et al., 2008; Guma et al., 2009; Shen et al., 2010; Kaikai et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2012; Du et al., 2013; Salvucci et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Studies of leptomeningeal collateral arteries in the brain have provided evidence that these collaterals form during embryonic development starting at approximately E13.5 as sprout-like extensions of endothelial cells from arterioles of existing cerebral artery trees.
source: Studies of the development of leptomeningeal (or pial) collaterals that interconnect the medial, anterior and posterior cerebral artery trees in the brain have provided evidence that these collaterals form during embryonic development starting at ~E13.5 as sprout-like extensions of endothelial cells from arterioles of existing cerebral artery trees (Lucitti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published studies, supported by citation.

claim: Nascent pial collateral vessels appear to course above the pial capillary plexus and fuse with an arteriole from an adjacent arterial tree.
source: These nascent vessels appear to course above the pial capillary plexus and fuse with an arteriole from an adjacent arterial tree (Lucitti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published studies, supported by citation.

claim: By E15.5, a portion of pial collaterals have acquired expression of the arterial marker EphrinB2.
source: By E15.5, a portion of these collaterals have acquired expression of the arterial marker EphrinB2 (Chalothorn and Faber, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published studies, supported by citation.

claim: Pial collateral density peaks around E18.5 and is followed by extensive remodeling, maturation and pruning that continues postnatally, achieving adult form and density by P21.
source: Pial collateral density peaks ~E18.5 and is followed by extensive remodeling, maturation and pruning that continues postnatally, achieving adult form and density by P21 (Chalothorn and Faber, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published studies, supported by citation.

claim: The formation of properly organized vascular networks is essential for function and requires the coordinated interaction of numerous factors and signaling pathways that regulate diverse cellular processes.
source: The formation of properly organized vascular networks is essential for function and requires the coordinated interaction of numerous factors and signaling pathways that regulate diverse cellular processes.
evidence: This is a general statement about vascular development based on established knowledge.

claim: VEGF signaling promotes endothelial cell survival, proliferation and motility.
source: VEGF signaling promotes endothelial cell survival, proliferation and motility while Dll4–Notch signaling suppresses VEGF signaling, in part, by regulating VEGFR expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VEGF signaling.

claim: Dll4–Notch signaling suppresses VEGF signaling, in part, by regulating VEGFR expression.
source: VEGF signaling promotes endothelial cell survival, proliferation and motility while Dll4–Notch signaling suppresses VEGF signaling, in part, by regulating VEGFR expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Notch signaling.

claim: Interactions between VEGF and Notch signaling underlie the specification of endothelial cell phenotypes during angiogenesis, including highly motile tip cells that extend numerous filopodia and trailing stalk cells with low motility that form the lumen of nascent tubules.
source: These interactions between VEGF and Notch signaling underly the specification of endothelial cell phenotypes during angiogenesis, including highly motile tip cells that extend numerous filopodia and trailing stalk cells with low motility that form the lumen of nascent tubules (Roca and Adams, 2007; Phng and Gerhardt, 2009; Eilken and Adams, 2010; Jakobsson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about tip/stalk cell specification, supported by citations.

claim: The proper specification and interplay of tip and stalk cells is essential for the orchestration of sprouting angiogenesis that mediates expansion of vascular networks.
source: The proper specification and interplay of tip and stalk cells is essential for the orchestration of sprouting angiogenesis that mediates expansion of vascular networks.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the importance of tip/stalk cell dynamics.

claim: VEGF and Notch signaling are critical for formation of the native collateral circulation.
source: Moreover, VEGF and Notch signaling are also critical for formation of the native collateral circulation (Cristofaro et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MLK – JNK signaling regulates tip cell identity and filopodia dynamics during retinal vascular development.
source: Studies of retinal vascular development demonstrate that MLK – JNK signaling regulates tip cell identity, and filopodia dynamics (Figure 6).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the retinal phenotype data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Defects in the MLK – JNK signaling pathway cause excessive sprouting angiogenesis characterized by an increased number of tips and filopodia, increased vascular density, and decreased expression of the Notch ligand Dll4 at the angiogenic front.
source: Consequently, defects in the MLK – JNK signaling pathway cause excessive sprouting angiogenesis characterized by an increased number of tips and filopodia, increased vascular density, and decreased expression of the Notch ligand Dll4 at the angiogenic front (Figure 7).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the retinal and molecular data presented in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Excessive sprouting angiogenesis may contribute to the critical requirement for MLK – JNK signaling during native collateral artery development.
source: Excessive sprouting angiogenesis may contribute to the critical requirement for MLK – JNK signaling during native collateral artery development (Figure 5) and this phenotype may result from promotion of Dll4 expression by MLK – JNK signaling (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the hypersprouting phenotype to collateral artery defects.

claim: The hypersprouting phenotype in JNK-deficient mice may result from promotion of Dll4 expression by MLK – JNK signaling.
source: Excessive sprouting angiogenesis may contribute to the critical requirement for MLK – JNK signaling during native collateral artery development (Figure 5) and this phenotype may result from promotion of Dll4 expression by MLK – JNK signaling (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed reduction in Dll4 expression in JNK-deficient cells.

claim: Defects in Notch signaling, including loss of Dll4, cause excessive endothelial cell sprouting during retinal vasculature development.
source: Indeed, it is established that defects in Notch signaling, including loss of Dll4 (Hellström et al., 2007), Notch1 (Hellström et al., 2007), Lfng (Benedito et al., 2009), RBP-J (Dou et al., 2008; Izumi et al., 2012) or chemical inhibition of γ-secretase (Hellström et al., 2007), cause excessive endothelial cell sprouting during retinal vasculature development.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The decreased Dll4 expression caused by JNK-deficiency in the vascular endothelium promotes excessive sprouting angiogenesis that disrupts the development of muscle collateral vessels.
source: These data support the conclusion that the decreased Dll4 expression caused by JNK-deficiency in the vascular endothelium promotes excessive sprouting angiogenesis that disrupts the development of muscle collateral vessels (Figure 8).
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion of the study, supported by the data and presented in a model in Figure 8.

claim: Human germ-line mutations in JNK pathway genes may contribute to an increased risk for poor outcomes in patients following exposure to an ischemic insult.
source: Moreover, our analysis suggests that human germ-line mutations in JNK pathway genes may contribute to an increased risk for poor outcomes in patients following exposure to an ischemic insult.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical implications of the findings.
